questions.stem_markdown: A 15-year-old comes to an adolescent clinic with his mother. When you are about to use CRAFFT, his mother answers the questions for him and he becomes guarded. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue with CRAFFT and accept the mother's answers where needed.
Pause and engage the adolescent directly, discussing confidentiality before using CRAFFT.
Switch to AUDIT-C instead of addressing the interaction first.
Skip screening today and wait until substance dependence is more obvious.
Move straight to neurocognitive assessment before taking a substance history.

questions.explanation_markdown: The Louisa notes place engagement and discussion of confidentiality at the start of a comprehensive adolescent drug and alcohol assessment. In a guarded young person, the best next step is to engage them directly and clarify confidentiality before proceeding with screening.

why_others_wrong.A: This bypasses the note-based emphasis on engaging the adolescent directly and discussing confidentiality.
why_others_wrong.C: AUDIT-C is an alcohol-specific tool in the notes, but it does not replace appropriate engagement and confidentiality discussion before screening.
why_others_wrong.D: The notes support screening and brief intervention rather than waiting for dependence to become obvious.
why_others_wrong.E: Neurocognitive assessment may be part of a broader assessment later, but it is not the best immediate step before basic engagement and screening.

key_takeaways: Substance-use assessment should begin with engagement.
Discussing confidentiality is part of adolescent drug and alcohol assessment.
Screening tools do not replace good adolescent communication.

questions.stem_markdown: A clinician asks a 16-year-old how often she vapes, then immediately says, "You should quit," without exploring readiness to change or whether there are signs of dependence. Within the 5 A's framework, which element was skipped?

options.text: Ask about current use
Advise quitting
Assess stage of change and dependence
Arrange follow-up
Assist with cessation support such as NRT

questions.explanation_markdown: In the 5 A's listed in the Louisa notes, Assess specifically covers stage of change and dependence. The clinician has asked about use and moved straight to advice, so the missed element is assessment of readiness and dependence.

why_others_wrong.A: The stem says the clinician has already asked about current use.
why_others_wrong.B: The clinician has already given advice to quit.
why_others_wrong.D: Arrange follow-up comes later in the framework and is not the key step omitted before the advice in this scenario.
why_others_wrong.E: Assistance also comes later; the immediate gap in the stem is failure to assess stage of change and dependence.

key_takeaways: The 5 A's include Ask, Assess, Advise, Assist and Arrange.
Assess covers stage of change and dependence.
Brief intervention should be tailored, not rushed straight into advice.

questions.stem_markdown: A 16-year-old says, "I barely drink, but I sometimes take a friend's sedative after big nights. That has to be lower risk than alcohol because not many teenagers do it." Which response is most supported by the notes?

options.text: Less common substances are usually lower priority than alcohol in adolescent review.
Occasional sedative use can usually be ignored unless tobacco is also involved.
Smaller percentages of adolescents use amphetamine-type substances and sedatives, but their harms are often greater, so this still needs careful assessment.
Sedatives are mainly relevant only when they are prescribed to the young person.
The main issue is only whether the sedative was taken for sleep rather than recreation.

questions.explanation_markdown: The Louisa notes state that although smaller percentages of adolescents use amphetamine-type substances and sedatives, their harms are often greater. That means infrequent or less common sedative use should not be dismissed as low priority.

why_others_wrong.A: This is the opposite of the note-based point that less commonly used substances can carry greater harm.
why_others_wrong.B: The notes do not make tobacco co-use the threshold for taking sedative use seriously.
why_others_wrong.D: The concern in the notes is harm from the substance, not whether it was prescribed to the young person.
why_others_wrong.E: The notes do not restrict concern to the reason the sedative was taken.

key_takeaways: Lower prevalence does not mean lower risk.
Sedatives are specifically highlighted as potentially more harmful despite less frequent use.
Adolescent substance-use review should not focus only on alcohol and tobacco.

questions.stem_markdown: A 17-year-old binge drinks most Saturdays and says his poor concentration at school on Wednesday cannot be alcohol-related because he is sober by then. Which reply is best supported by the notes?

options.text: Once the immediate intoxication has passed, concentration should be back to normal.
Lingering cognitive effects mainly occur only with daily alcohol dependence.
Binge drinking is mainly important only if it leads to obvious withdrawal.
Teenage drinking can affect memory and concentration even up to a week later, so this pattern is still relevant.
Alcohol matters less here because overall youth alcohol use has been declining.

questions.explanation_markdown: The CAH Bible notes that teenage drinking affects memory and concentration even up to 1 week later. Louisa also notes that adolescents are more likely to binge drink and suffer harms. So midweek concentration problems cannot be dismissed simply because the young person is no longer intoxicated.

why_others_wrong.A: This contradicts the CAH Bible, which notes that cognitive effects can persist beyond the period of intoxication.
why_others_wrong.B: The notes do not restrict these effects to daily dependence.
why_others_wrong.C: The Louisa notes describe binge drinking and harms as important concerns even without obvious withdrawal.
why_others_wrong.E: Declining overall use does not make an individual binge-drinking pattern clinically unimportant.

key_takeaways: Binge drinking in adolescents can have harms beyond the night of use.
Memory and concentration may be affected for days after teenage drinking.
Being sober at review does not rule out alcohol-related cognitive impact.

questions.stem_markdown: A 15-year-old uses cannabis most evenings and says, "I've never been paranoid or hallucinated, so it can't be affecting my schoolwork." Which response is best supported by the notes?

options.text: Without psychotic symptoms, cannabis is unlikely to affect cognition.
Early cannabis use is linked to impaired attention, memory and concentration, so school problems can still be relevant even without psychotic symptoms.
Cannabis mainly changes appetite and sleep rather than attention or memory.
Cognitive effects only become important once withdrawal symptoms appear.
If use is limited to the evening, study performance is usually unaffected.

questions.explanation_markdown: The Louisa notes state that early-onset cannabis increases the risk of impaired attention, IQ, memory and concentration, while the CAH Bible also describes poor cognitive development with cannabis use. Psychotic symptoms are not required for cognition and schoolwork to be affected.

why_others_wrong.A: The notes explicitly link cannabis with cognitive harms beyond psychosis.
why_others_wrong.C: This understates the note-based concerns about attention, memory, judgement and cognition.
why_others_wrong.D: Withdrawal is a separate issue and is not required before cognitive harm becomes relevant.
why_others_wrong.E: The notes do not support reassurance based on evening-only use.

key_takeaways: Cannabis can affect cognition even without paranoia or hallucinations.
Early cannabis use is linked to impaired attention, memory and concentration.
School difficulties can be relevant to cannabis counselling.

questions.stem_markdown: A 17-year-old is brought to the ED after smoking cannabis. He is anxious, says "nothing feels real," and believes people nearby are watching him. Which explanation best fits the notes?

options.text: Acute cannabis effects with derealisation and paranoia
Cannabis withdrawal
Normal adolescent stress without substance-specific features
Alcohol withdrawal
A primary sleep disorder

questions.explanation_markdown: The CAH Bible lists anxiety, restlessness, derealisation, depersonalisation, paranoia, hallucinations and psychosis among cannabis effects. In a young person who has just smoked cannabis, derealisation and suspiciousness fit acute cannabis effects better than withdrawal or unrelated stress.

why_others_wrong.B: Louisa's withdrawal features include irritability, anxiety, anorexia, vivid dreams and restlessness after cessation, not this acute post-use presentation with derealisation and paranoia.
why_others_wrong.C: The symptom cluster is specifically described as part of cannabis effects in the notes.
why_others_wrong.D: The scenario is temporally linked to cannabis use, and the note-based features point toward cannabis rather than alcohol withdrawal.
why_others_wrong.E: A sleep disorder does not explain the acute onset of derealisation and paranoia after cannabis use.

key_takeaways: Cannabis can cause acute anxiety and perceptual disturbance.
Derealisation and paranoia are listed cannabis effects.
Timing in relation to substance use helps distinguish acute effects from withdrawal.
